Yes, after far too long Michael Stewart and Jerry Herman’s 1964 musical Hello, Dolly! has returned to London’s West End for a limited season at the London Palladium. As the 19th becomes the 20th century, Dolly Levi (Imelda Staunton) is back in New York and up to mischief.
The production’s knockabout energy sends the soul soaring.
Cooke and company have seized an old-fashioned show, unexpectedly provided vanishingly rare but hugely welcome genuine charm, and made it zing.
For all those who love this great Broadway musical, the present revival is not to be missed.
This is a big, spectacular show that carries you away to a bygone era.

The much beloved 1969 film version of HELLO DOLLY directed by dance legend and renowned perfectionist Gene Kelly, ran-up huge budget over-spends through its extravagant sets, and costumes for hundreds of extras. It also substantially overran its original shooting schedule to the extent, that the movie nearly bankrupted 20th Century Fox studios.
Staunton’s Dolly is a force of nature, running rings around Andy Nyman’s blustering Horace to deliver the star turn that keeps this show on the road.
This is one case where every element came together beautifully to create pure theatre magic and the result is one of the best shows of the year.
This terrific Hello, Dolly! is a reminder of the power of musical theatre to lift spirits and touch hearts.

But there is no denying the powerhouse performance of Imelda Staunton who embraces the role with characteristic energy and intelligence, bringing light and shade to Dolly that only a serious actor at the top of her game could achieve.

It’s best when it bolts along and veers away from sentimentality, and Staunton gets this: she always has a glint in her eye that shows she’s in on the joke. Oh, and she can sing! She belts the titular track in act two in a way that makes you feel perplexed as to why she hasn’t done much more of this...

cn.t: Staunton delivers a powerhouse, award-worthy performance in Cooke's lavish revival, bringing unexpected emotional depth and sincerity to the classic musical. Critics hail it as a sumptuous, roof-raising spectacle and the West End event of the summer.
